approachQuestion.prompt:
Route markers

A route is recorded as an ordered list of integer points. Count how many consecutive triples make a strict left turn: for points P[i], P[i+1], P[i+2], count the triple when the path from P[i] to P[i+1] turns counterclockwise toward P[i+2]. Collinear triples and triples containing repeated points do not count. Return the count; do not reorder or modify the route.

Example 1: [(0,0),(2,0),(2,3),(0,3)] -> 2.
Example 2: [(0,0),(1,1),(2,2),(2,1)] -> 0.
Example 3: [(0,0),(0,0),(1,0)] -> 0.
constraints: 3 <= n <= 200000, where n is the number of points.
Each x and y coordinate is an integer in [-10^9,10^9].
Use exact integer arithmetic. The count fits a signed 64-bit integer.
For each index i from 0 through n-3, classify exactly the triple (P[i],P[i+1],P[i+2]).

options.text: For each consecutive triple P[i], P[i+1], P[i+2], compute the signed cross product of the two vectors from P[i]. Count it only when the result is positive.
options.feedback: The sign distinguishes left turns; zero correctly excludes collinear triples, including repeated points.

options.text: For each consecutive triple, divide each vertical change by its horizontal change and count when the first slope is smaller than the second.
options.feedback: Vertical segments make division undefined, and equal horizontal coordinates can occur in valid inputs.

options.text: For each consecutive triple, compute the angle between the two vectors with floating-point trigonometry and count positive angles.
options.feedback: The angle magnitude is not the orientation sign, and near-collinear large-coordinate triples can lose the sign through rounding.

options.text: For every pair of positions i<j, inspect the triple beginning at i and count it when j=i+2 and its orientation is positive.
options.feedback: This can return the right count, but examines quadratic many index pairs to process a linear list of consecutive triples.

feedback.reason: The cross-product sign measures turn direction using vectors with the same origin.
details: For each three consecutive points, form the two vectors that start at the first point and end at the second and third. Multiply the first vector’s x component by the second vector’s y component, then subtract the first vector’s y component times the second vector’s x component. Count a positive result. A zero result is collinear and is not counted; a negative result turns the other way.

The cross-product sign measures turn direction using vectors with the same origin. Positive counts the requested turn; zero is collinear and must not count. Sorting points would destroy the route's consecutive-triple meaning.

“For each consecutive triple P[i], P[i+1], P[i+2], compute the signed cross product of the two vectors from P[i]. Count it only when the result is positive.”: The sign distinguishes left turns; zero correctly excludes collinear triples, including repeated points.

“For each consecutive triple, divide each vertical change by its horizontal change and count when the first slope is smaller than the second.”: Vertical segments make division undefined, and equal horizontal coordinates can occur in valid inputs.

“For each consecutive triple, compute the angle between the two vectors with floating-point trigonometry and count positive angles.”: The angle magnitude is not the orientation sign, and near-collinear large-coordinate triples can lose the sign through rounding.

“For every pair of positions i<j, inspect the triple beginning at i and count it when j=i+2 and its orientation is positive.”: This can return the right count, but examines quadratic many index pairs to process a linear list of consecutive triples.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For the fixed exact cross-product scan revealed after question 1, choose its tight worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair. Let n be the number of route points.
constraints: Auxiliary space includes temporary state and the call stack, but excludes supplied input and returned output.

options.text: O(n) time, O(log n) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: One exact orientation test per consecutive triple gives linear work.
details: The scan evaluates each consecutive triple once and stores only a fixed number of scalar values.
Every one of the n−2 consecutive triples may affect the returned count, so a worst-case input requires examining each triple. The scan uses constant work per triple.

Only the loop index, three point references or coordinate pairs, one cross-product value, and the running count are retained. There is no recursion or size-dependent auxiliary structure; the scalar count is the output.

Coordinates are integers in [-10^9,10^9]. Each coordinate difference lies in [-2·10^9,2·10^9]; each product magnitude is at most 4·10^18 and the cross-product difference magnitude at most 8·10^18, within signed 64-bit range. Compute differences and products in signed 64-bit arithmetic before subtraction. Floating-point and arbitrary-precision models are not assumed.
Iterative scan; fixed number of signed 64-bit words, no recursion. Input points and scalar output are excluded.
